title: intervalClassifiers: Intervals as Hypothesis Class
content:
An interval classifier on ℕ is parameterized by two endpoints $a \leq b$ and classifies $x$ as positive iff $a \leq x \leq b$. The definition includes 'empty' intervals where $a > b$ (which classify no point as positive), providing the all-negative witness for the ∅ subset in the shattering argument.

This family has VC dimension 2: strictly larger than threshold classifiers (VC dim 1) because we have two free parameters instead of one, and strictly smaller than the full power set because intervals are convex.

title: Four-Witness Lower Bound
content:
The lower bound proof case-splits on whether $a$ and $b$ belong to the target labeling $T$, producing four witnesses:

| $T$ | Witness interval | Rationale |
|-----|------------------|-----------|
| $\{a,b\}$ | $[a,b]$ | Contains both endpoints |
| $\{a\}$ | $[a,a]$ | Contains only $a$ |
| $\{b\}$ | $[b,b]$ | Contains only $b$ |
| $\emptyset$ | $[b+1,b]$ | Empty (since $b+1 > b$) |

This exhausts all $2^2 = 4$ labelings of $\{a,b\}$, proving $H_{int}$ shatters $\{a,b\}$.
mathContext: $\forall a < b$: 4 witnesses cover all $2^2 = 4$ subsets of $\{a,b\}$.

title: Convexity Obstruction for Triples
content:
The upper bound uses the adversarial labeling $T = \{a, c\}$ (include endpoints, exclude the middle element $b$). The argument:

1. If $[l,r]$ realizes $T$ on $\{a,b,c\}$, then $l \leq a$ (since $a \in T$) and $r \geq c$ (since $c \in T$).
2. Since $a < b < c$, we get $l \leq a < b < c \leq r$.
3. Therefore $l \leq b \leq r$, meaning $b \in [l,r]$.
4. But $b \notin T = \{a,c\}$ — contradiction.

This is the *convexity obstruction*: any interval is convex (contains all integers between its endpoints), so it cannot include two elements while skipping one in between.
mathContext: $l \leq a < b < c \leq r \Rightarrow l \leq b \wedge b \leq r$ — interval convexity forces $b \in [l,r]$.
